title: My police AI learned to chase me through a hyperloop. I described it in one sentence; coding agents measured, fixed and tested it
author: Away_Tour1488
selftext:
I'm making Wrecked District, a single-player car combat game in Rust and Bevy where a police pack hunts you through a generated city. Almost all of the code is written by AI coding agents (mostly Claude Code, some Codex). I design it, play it and make the calls; the agents write, measure and test. Six months, about 6,500 commits so far.

The clip is one of my runs from this morning. The town has hyperloop portals, and the pack dives in after me: 3 to 9 cars followed me on each of the 8 rides in that run. A month ago none of them did. It's the most typical example of how I work with agents, so here's how it went.

Oct 19 I wrote one sentence: "the bots still don't use the hyperloop, they don't even follow me."

Every match records itself, so the agent didn't guess. It went through my last 25 games: I'd taken a portal 5 times, a bot followed twice, both from far across town, and two bots right next to the entrance didn't move. The cause was that a bot could only plan a route into a station from the road graph, and the cars on my tail sit in the station's forecourt, off the graph. The fix was a direct path from wherever the car is into the bay.

Nov 18: "bots should take the portal if it gets them to me faster." Measured again: a quarter of the bots' rides ended farther from me than they started. The tube was compared against the car's current target point, which can jump across the map between plans, and a ride can't be undone. Now a tube only counts if it gets the car to me, not to its waypoint, no later than the road would.

Nov 19: the first follower went in 1.3 to 3.1 s after me. The pack only learned about my ride once the station had already taken me, so the car on my tail overshot the entrance and came back in a loop. Now "he's going in" means "he's aimed at the entrance and can't miss it", half a second earlier.

What keeps this workable is a handful of rules the agents read before every task. No fix without numbers from my own recordings, and every analysis leaves a permanent tool behind instead of a throwaway script (the follow lag is now a line in the default report). Fix the cause, failing test first; there are about 11,700 tests now. Every trap we hit goes into a known-issues log with its symptom, cause, rule and a guard test, 459 entries so far, and an agent has to read the file for its area before touching it. Context windows end, the files stay. Each agent works in its own git worktree, and builds and tests go through a scheduler across two machines so parallel agents don't trample each other.

Even the camera work in the clip is agent code: it's the game's own replay director. Today's fix was in it, because portal scenes rarely made it into the after-match replay. A town with \~117 moving bodies ate the replay's memory budget, and the jump through the tube made the director throw the shot away
